title: Binary Search
description: Brute force to optimized: a linear scan versus the classic binary search template, halving the range every step.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array nums sorted in ascending order and a target integer, return the index of target if it exists in nums, or -1 if it does not, in O(log n) time.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Since nums is sorted, comparing target to the middle element immediately reveals which half of the array could possibly contain it: if target is smaller, it can only be in the left half; if larger, only in the right half.

blocks.title: Analogy: Looking Up a Word in a Physical Dictionary
blocks.text: Picture flipping open a dictionary to roughly its middle. If the word you want comes alphabetically before what you see, you know to search only the earlier pages; if it comes after, only the later pages. Repeating this halves the remaining pages to check every time.

blocks.caption: Comparing target to the middle element discards half the remaining search range every step

blocks.text: Before scanning linearly, notice the sorted property lets a single comparison at the midpoint eliminate half the remaining candidates, which is the defining signal for binary search.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If nums[mid] equals target, the answer is found immediately.

Observation 2: If nums[mid] is less than target, since the array is sorted ascending, every index <= mid is also too small, so the search can safely move past mid.

Observation 3: Symmetrically, if nums[mid] is greater than target, every index >= mid is too large.

Observation 4: Repeating this halves the search range every step, converging on the target's position (or exhausting the range) in O(log n) steps.
This leads to standard binary search: maintain lo and hi bounds, compare nums[mid] to target, and narrow the range accordingly until found or the range is exhausted.
Scan the array from left to right, comparing each element to target directly.

items: Iterate over every index i from 0 to n-1.
If nums[i] equals target, return i.
If the loop completes without a match, return -1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A linear scan directly checks every element, correct regardless of whether the array is sorted.
It does not exploit the sorted property at all, costing O(n) even though O(log n) is achievable.

blocks.text: Limitation: the sorted property is never used; binary search exploits it to eliminate half the remaining candidates every step, achieving O(log n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why scanning is unnecessary: a single comparison at the midpoint tells you definitively which half of a SORTED array could contain the target, making the other half provably irrelevant.

How the search narrows: maintain lo and hi; compute mid; if nums[mid] equals target, done; if less, move lo to mid+1; if greater, move hi to mid-1.

Termination: the search ends either by finding the target, or when lo exceeds hi (target absent).

The core idea: repeatedly halve the search range using the sorted order, the textbook binary search algorithm.
Maintain lo=0, hi=n-1. Compute mid, compare nums[mid] to target, and narrow the range accordingly until found or the range is exhausted.

blocks.caption: Binary search halves the range every step using the sorted order

blocks.text: Since nums is sorted ascending, nums[mid] correctly partitions the array: everything before mid is smaller, everything after is larger. Comparing target against nums[mid] therefore reliably determines which half to keep searching, and discarding the other half never loses the target if it exists, guaranteeing correctness while halving the search space every step.

blocks.text: Binary Search is the foundational template every other binary-search-based problem builds on: exploit sorted order to halve the search range every step.

items: Using mid = (lo + hi) / 2 without considering integer overflow in languages with fixed-width integers (mitigated via lo + (hi-lo)/2).
Off-by-one errors in the loop condition (lo <= hi) or the range updates (mid+1, mid-1).

blocks.text: Stating the loop invariant clearly ("target, if present, is always within [lo, hi]") helps avoid subtle off-by-one bugs.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "sorted array, find in O(log n)", think: binary search, halve the range using the midpoint comparison.

items: How would you handle duplicate values, finding the first or last occurrence?
How would you adapt this for a rotated sorted array?
Search in Rotated Sorted Array, First Bad Version, and countless other binary-search-based problems all build on this exact template.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear scan runs in O(n) time; binary search runs in O(log n) time, both using O(1) space.

items: Core Idea: compare target to the middle element; discard the half that cannot contain it; repeat.
Time: O(n) for linear scan, O(log n) for binary search.
Most Important Observation: sorted order lets a single comparison eliminate half the remaining search space.
Interview Difficulty: the essential building block for every other binary search problem.
One line memory trick: compare to the middle, discard the wrong half, repeat.
